scope: Yeah. I think the experiment is telling you something fairly clear:  **MoA is not fixing the kind of failure Hermes actually has.**  The failures we’ve been watching are mostly not:  > “DeepSeek couldn’t reason through this technical problem.”  They’re:  > “the system gave a model stale/contradictory state, asked the wrong question, allowed the wrong transition, then treated another model’s opinion as progress.”  Adding 6.1 Sol plus an Ollama Cloud adviser on top of that can just produce **more sophisticated agreement about the wrong abstraction**.  A babysitter only helps if it has something meaningfully different to do. If both models receive a 500-line polluted card history and are effectively asked “what next?”, you get:  ```text worker:   concludes X  adviser:   reviews X in same broken frame   suggests caveats / extra validation  aggregator:   turns caveats into more work ```  Which is basically what Hermes has been doing already.  The useful form of MoA would be much narrower:  ```text DeepSeek / Codex:     perform bounded technical work  6.1 Sol:     propose result / next state  adviser:     ONLY try to falsify:       - is this work already done?       - is there actually a worker-executable action?       - is this authority missing?       - does this create duplicate work?       - does this violate a lifecycle invariant?  deterministic controller:     apply hard rules     decide transition ```  The adviser should not be “another smart agent with opinions”. It should be a **hostile state-transition auditor**.  And critically, it should receive a compact canonical object, not the whole archaeological dig:  ```yaml accepted_evidence:   - ... completed_actions:   - ... remaining_actions:   - ... operator_authority:   live_test: false worker_executable_actions: [] current_dependencies:   - ... proposed_transition: WAITING ```  Then ask exactly:  > “Can you identify any evidence that this transition is invalid? Do not propose new work unless an accepted requirement is demonstrably unsatisfied.”  That might actually help.  But I would **not** use MoA to compensate for DeepSeek being the executive controller. The pruning fiasco shows why: once the harness thinks “nonterminal = needs reasoning”, three smart models can spend half a million tokens rediscovering that nothing should happen.  Given what you’ve seen today, my current hierarchy would be:  ```text 5.6 Sol   executive / board grooming / lifecycle judgement  DeepSeek / Codex   implementation, forensics, bounded technical tasks  6.1 Sol   hostile review, bug finding, regression design  Ollama-cloud adviser   optional falsifier at high-value decision boundaries only ```  Rather than:  ```text DeepSeek   does work  6.1 Sol + cloud adviser   babysit it continuously ```  Because continuous supervision is expensive and seems to encourage **epistemic bureaucracy** rather than better decisions.  The experiment I’d run now is very small: take 10 of the horrible real cards we’ve already debugged and compare:  1. 5.6 Sol alone on a canonical state summary. 2. 6.1 Sol alone. 3. 6.1 Sol + one adviser. 4. DeepSeek + one adviser.  Score only:  ```text correct state correct next action unnecessary worker launched? missed executable work? invented dependency? operator gate respected? tokens used ```  Not prose quality. Not “interesting insights”.  My suspicion is that **the adviser adds much less than simply having the right executive model plus hard invariants**.  And if that’s true, MoA is probably best reserved for genuinely contested technical judgements, not routine Kanban control.
